html:
A Roofing Sub That Doesn't Slow Down Your Schedule

General contractors bidding institutional and commercial work across the Triad need a roofing sub who turns numbers around on bid day, holds to a spec without a redline fight, and hands over a closeout package the owner's rep signs off on the first pass. That is the role we fill on projects from Innovation Quarter build-outs downtown to industrial park work in Kernersville and Union Cross, and it's the same standard we hold on smaller tenant improvement jobs where the roof scope is a small line item in a much bigger contract.

Bid-Day Responsiveness

A late roofing number holds up an entire bid package. We work from the drawings and spec section a GC sends over, not a phone estimate, and we turn a firm number around inside the bid window the project actually gives us, including alternates and unit pricing when the owner's spec calls for them.

When addenda come out late in the bid cycle, we revise and resend rather than asking the GC to assume our original number still holds. That matters most on public and institutional work, where a bid protest over an outdated sub number is a real risk nobody wants to carry.

We also break out value-engineering alternates when a GC asks for them, showing the cost and warranty tradeoff of a recover system against a full tear-off, or a lower-slope membrane change, in plain terms an estimator can hand straight to the owner without reformatting.

Working to the Spec as Written

Institutional roof specs in North Carolina reference a base building code, ASCE 7 wind uplift design pressures, and often a specific manufacturer's system by name. We submit product data sheets, fastening patterns, and warranty terms that match the spec section directly, and where a substitution makes sense, we document the equivalency with side-by-side performance data rather than asking the architect to take our word for it.

That discipline carries into the submittal review cycle. We track RFIs and shop drawing comments the same way the GC's project engineer does, so a roofing question doesn't sit unanswered for weeks while the rest of the building envelope moves forward around it and the schedule float quietly disappears.

Coordinating With the Trades Above and Below Us

A roof is rarely finished in isolation. Rooftop mechanical curbs, electrical conduit penetrations, and fall protection anchor points all have to land before or during roof installation, not after. We coordinate directly with the GC's mechanical and electrical subs on curb locations and penetration sequencing so the roof doesn't get opened back up two weeks after it's dried in.

On a multi-trade schedule, we also flag long-lead material orders, particularly standing seam metal panels and PVC membrane runs, early enough that a roofing delay doesn't become the item holding up substantial completion.

Fall protection anchor placement gets coordinated with the GC's safety manager before other trades need roof access for their own rooftop equipment installs, so a mechanical or electrical crew isn't waiting on us to open a tie-off point mid-schedule.

What Our Closeout Package Includes

Closeout is where a lot of roofing subs lose time at the end of a project. We build our package to clear owner review on the first submission:

  • Manufacturer warranty registration completed and submitted, not left as a pending item
  • As-built roof drawings matched to what was actually installed, including approved substitutions
  • Material submittals and product data sheets organized by roof section
  • Final inspection report from the manufacturer where the warranty tier requires one
  • Punch list items closed and documented with photos before final payment request

Bonding, Insurance, and Safety Documentation

Institutional and public work carries bonding and insurance requirements that vary by project size and owner. We carry the coverage levels most Triad institutional work requires and provide certificates and bonding documentation in the format a GC's project accountant needs before mobilization, not after a request chases us down.

Safety documentation follows the same standard. Fall protection plans, hot-work permits, and site-specific safety submittals go out with our proposal, not as an afterthought once the GC's safety manager asks for them.

Where a project carries builder's risk coverage through the GC or owner, we provide the roofing-specific information that policy typically requires, including membrane type, fire rating, and staged completion dates for phased work, so the GC's insurance broker isn't chasing that detail down separately.

Questions General Contractors Ask Us

How fast can you turn around a bid number?

We work directly from drawings and spec sections and typically return a firm number within the bid window the project provides, including revisions when addenda come out late.

Do you work to manufacturer-specified systems named in the spec?

Yes, and where a substitution is warranted we document the equivalency for the architect's review rather than asking for a verbal exception.

Can you coordinate directly with our mechanical and electrical subs?

We coordinate curb locations, penetration sequencing, and anchor point placement directly with the trades above and below roofing so the roof isn't reopened after it's installed.

What's included in your closeout package?

Warranty registration, as-built drawings, organized submittals, a manufacturer inspection report where required, and documented punch list closeout, built to clear owner review on the first pass.

Do you carry the bonding and insurance our projects require?

We carry coverage levels sized to institutional and public commercial work in this region and provide documentation ahead of mobilization rather than in response to a request.
